title: A reading plan
hook: a little each day or week: Ezra read the law to the people from morning to midday, then day by day through the feast
tomorrow: what did Thoreau read each morning beside a frozen pond?

segments.voice: My book: Augustine read one line and stopped, and Alypius read on and found his own. Now, how to keep reading it.

A book bought with real hope can sit on the nightstand for a year, a receipt still marking page twelve. Another gets swallowed in one weekend and forgotten by Tuesday. The book of Nehemiah has a reading that went another way. The people of Jerusalem gathered in the street before the water gate and asked Ezra the scribe to bring out the book of the law. He read it aloud "from the morning until midday." And then he didn't stop there.
screen: `PAGE TWELVE FOR A YEAR.` → `THE STREET BY THE WATER GATE.` → `FROM MORNING UNTIL MIDDAY.`

segments.voice: First, the way they read: "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading." Not just loud. Clear, with helpers explaining what it meant. The people wept as they heard it, and their leaders told them: go, eat and drink and send portions to those who have nothing, for this day is holy. Then the line that answers the question: "Also day by day, from the first day unto the last day, he read in the book of the law of God." Day by day, through the whole feast. Not one heroic sitting. A portion each day, explained, then lived. That rhythm runs through Jewish practice. In synagogues, the Torah is read aloud in public, a portion at a time; the book of Acts mentions Moses being read in the synagogues every Sabbath day. A little, regularly, together, with someone to give the sense. A reading plan on your own path can borrow all three: a set portion, a set time, and someone to ask what it means.

segments.voice: Open something you're reading, or recall a line you know well. Read one short passage aloud, slowly and distinctly, then say in your own words what it means. Sit quietly with that sense for the rest of the sit.
A reading plan: a set portion at a set time, a little each day or week, like Ezra's reading day by day through the feast.
